title: A Comparative Study of News Exposure and Consumption On and Off Facebook
screen_reason: Browser-extension panel of 642 US Prolific users (12 weeks, November 2020 - February 2021) donating 123,995 news posts seen on desktop Facebook and 70,587 news article visits off Facebook, with sources labelled misinformation/not by Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard. Reports the share of news items from misinformation sources on Facebook (5.9%) and off it (2.6%), and the share of users exposed at least once (63% on, 46% off).

estimates.measure_type: % of news-related posts users were shown on their Facebook timeline that came from sources labelled as spreading misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 5.9% of news exposure posts ... originate from misinformation news sources
estimates.denominator: 123,995 news-related posts received on desktop Facebook timelines by the panel (a post counts as news if published by a news media Facebook page or if its landing URL is one of 4,149 news domains)
estimates.definition: The post's source domain carries a 'misinformation' quality label from Media Bias Fact Check or NewsGuard (456 of the 4,149 listed news websites)
estimates.misinfo_def: "sources labeled as repeatedly sharing misinformation by Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard"
estimates.source_quote: We find that 5.9% of news exposure posts and 2.6% of news consumption articles in our dataset originate from misinformation news sources.
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.2 'Prevalence of misinformation on and off Facebook', CSCW359:9; also abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Third-party source-level ratings: Media Bias Fact Check (2,062 sites) and NewsGuard (2,939 sites) combined into 4,149 outlets; 456 carry a misinformation quality label, 2,309 a factual label. No article-level verification and no inter-rater statistic; the authors state the same label is applied to every item from a given source.
estimates.moderator_quote: Note that these labels are applied at the news source level. Hence, we assign the same value to all news items originating from a given source. We acknowledge this as a limitation of our work
estimates.notes: Aggregate item-level share (all posts pooled), not a per-user average. The authors explicitly call it an upper bound: 'not all content from these sources is necessarily false. Thus, this 5.9% should be considered an upper bound.' Denominator is news content only, and only news from the 4,149-domain list; desktop browsing only, no mobile.

estimates.platform: news media websites visited off Facebook (desktop browsing)
estimates.measure_type: % of news articles users visited on news media websites off Facebook that came from sources labelled as spreading misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 2.6% of news consumption articles ... originate from misinformation news sources
estimates.denominator: 70,587 news article URLs visited off Facebook across 1,882 news domains by the panel via desktop browsers
estimates.definition: The visited article's source domain carries a 'misinformation' quality label from Media Bias Fact Check or NewsGuard
estimates.misinfo_def: "sources labeled as repeatedly sharing misinformation by Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard"
estimates.n: 70,587 news article visits (467 users; 13 users visiting >100 articles/day were excluded as abnormal)
estimates.source_quote: We find that 5.9% of news exposure posts and 2.6% of news consumption articles in our dataset originate from misinformation news sources.
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.2 'Prevalence of misinformation on and off Facebook', CSCW359:9; also abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same Media Bias Fact Check + NewsGuard source-level labelling (456 misinformation sites of 4,149 listed).
estimates.moderator_quote: In total, the dataset contains 70,587 news article URLs visited across 1,882 news domains. In median, each user accessed 38 news articles
estimates.notes: Off-platform counterpart of the 5.9% Facebook row; same panel, same labelling, different platform, hence a separate row. Denominator is news article visits only (not all web visits), so it is a news-diet share, not a share of all browsing. Same source-level upper-bound caveat applies.

estimates.measure_type: % of panel users exposed to at least one post from a misinformation source on Facebook
estimates.value_raw: 63% of users were exposed to misinformation at least once on Facebook
estimates.denominator: Panel users with Facebook news-post data (467 per Section 2.2; Table 1 lists 416 users with on-Facebook data)
estimates.definition: At least one news post received on the Facebook timeline came from a domain with a misinformation label
estimates.misinfo_def: "sources labeled as repeatedly sharing misinformation by Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard"
estimates.n: 467 users (see notes: the paper gives 467 for both on- and off-Facebook data, while Table 1 lists 416 on-Facebook)
estimates.source_quote: The figure shows that 63% of users were exposed to misinformation at least once on Facebook, while 46% of users consumed misinformation at least once off Facebook.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Media Bias Fact Check + NewsGuard source-level labels.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our analysis is based on data collected from 642 users recruited on Prolific [98] between November 2020 and February 2021 during and immediately after the U.S. Presidential Election. The user sample is not representative
estimates.notes: Confidence is medium only because of the denominator: Section 2.2 states 123,995 posts 'received by 467 users' but Table 1 lists 416 users with on-Facebook data, and the exact N behind Fig. 3 is not restated. The reach threshold is one post over a 12-week desktop-only window, so it is an at-least-once figure for a restricted channel.

estimates.platform: news media websites visited off Facebook (desktop browsing)
estimates.measure_type: % of panel users who visited at least one article from a misinformation source off Facebook
estimates.value_raw: 46% of users consumed misinformation at least once off Facebook
estimates.denominator: Panel users with off-Facebook browsing data (467 users after excluding 13 with >100 article visits per day)
estimates.definition: At least one news article visited off Facebook came from a domain with a misinformation label
estimates.misinfo_def: "sources labeled as repeatedly sharing misinformation by Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard"
estimates.source_quote: The figure shows that 63% of users were exposed to misinformation at least once on Facebook, while 46% of users consumed misinformation at least once off Facebook.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Media Bias Fact Check + NewsGuard source-level labels.
estimates.moderator_quote: For the regression analysis, we applied an additional activity threshold to ensure meaningful data. Specifically, we included only users who visited at least 10 URLs. This filter yielded a final sample of 69,862 URLs received by 467 users with sufficient off Facebook browsing activity.
estimates.notes: Behavioural at-least-once reach over 12 weeks of desktop browsing only; deliberate visits, so 'consumed' rather than merely seen. Same denominator ambiguity as the Facebook reach row.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Per-user distributional statistics not extracted as separate rows, though verbatim: on Facebook the median user's misinformation fraction is 2% (mean 6%, SD 12%), off Facebook the median is 0% (mean 3%, SD 8%). These are user-level counterparts of the 5.9%/2.6% aggregate rows; an adjudicator may want them as extra EXPOSURE rows. 2) No CONCENTRATION row is possible. The closest statement - 'misinformation posts represent a small fraction (less than 20%) of news exposure on Facebook for the majority of users 92%, a small subset 1% encounters a much higher proportion 60% of misinformation' - describes the misinformation fraction WITHIN the top users' own feeds, not the share of all misinformation exposure that those users account for, so R1 (needs both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct) cannot be met. 3) Comparative statistics are not prevalence shares: '72% of users encounter equal or more misinformation on Facebook than off it', '22% of users experience twice the amount', '53% of users who never consumed misinformation off Facebook were exposed at least once to it on the platform', mean on-off difference 0.03. 4) Referral shares are not prevalence: 'only 4% of users' news consumption off Facebook is driven by news exposure on Facebook, and only 5.7% of misinformation consumption off Facebook is driven by news exposure on Facebook'. 5) Political-bias shares (43% of exposure posts and 36% of consumption URLs from left-leaning sources; 11% and 6% from right-leaning; 22% vs 36% of users seeing a single political leaning) are ideology, not veracity. 6) 456 of 4,149 listed news websites carry a misinformation label - a property of the rating list, not of what users saw. 7) Volume figures (median 3 news posts/active day on Facebook, 2 articles off; 6 vs 40 seconds median attention) are not misinformation shares. 8) Regression coefficients in Tables 2-5 (e.g. Republican partisanship 0.40, authoritarian attitudes -0.32) are associations, not prevalence.

rob.design: Browser-extension data donation panel: 642 US users recruited on Prolific between November 2020 and February 2021 (during and immediately after the US presidential election), asked to keep a desktop extension active for 6 weeks over a 12-week collection window and to complete five surveys. Sample explicitly non-representative (65% female vs 51% in the US population; 79% white; recruited across 48 states); no response rate; attrition means different Ns per analysis (Table 1: 467 off-Facebook, 416 on-Facebook, 304 completing all surveys). Exposure measured directly from rendered page content plus visibility time, not self-reported or inferred. Desktop only, no mobile. Misinformation coded at the SOURCE level from Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard (4,149 news domains, 456 misinformation-labelled), with the same label applied to every item from a source; no article-level verification, no inter-rater reliability statistic, and the authors state the resulting 5.9% is an upper bound. 13 users with >100 article visits per day excluded as abnormal. IRB-approved and GDPR-compliant; code and survey instruments on GitHub.
rob.item6_quote: Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard evaluate the political bias and factual accuracy of the news sources they list. We leverage their data to assign each source in our list a quality label (misinformation or not) and a political bias label (left, center, or right). ... based on ratings from Media Bias Fact Check and NewsGuard, we have 456 news websites with a misinformation quality label and 2,309 with a factual quality label.
rob.item10_quote: We find that 5.9% of news exposure posts and 2.6% of news consumption articles in our dataset originate from misinformation news sources.
